svg.title: PNP P032 walkthrough — Products priced above their category average
svg.desc: Products filter, one-row category average CTE, scalar benchmark, strict comparison and final output.
svg.text: Why does Juice clear the Beverages benchmark?
Follow the same four Products rows through the saved learner query.
ƒ = calculated from Products · ▸ = focus row
FROM Products supplies one candidate row per catalogue product because every requested output field and every
price comes from this table. The first CTE then keeps only CategoryID 5009; no second source is required.
▸ Rows 1–3 remain; Bread (CategoryID 5010) is filtered out.
required_table · one row per eligible Beverages product
Why does avg_sale_price return one row?
AVG reads every known Sale_Price in required_table, including Tea and Coffee even though they will not pass
the later filter. An aggregate without GROUP BY collapses the three product rows into one category benchmark.
One CTE row = one benchmark for the selected category, not one row per product.
Why repeat the scalar beside each product?
The outer SELECT starts from required_table, so its three product rows remain the report candidates. The
scalar subquery reads the one-row avg_sale_price CTE and places 200.00 beside each product; there is no join
because this is one shared scalar.
The strict comparison removes Tea (100 < 200) and Coffee (200 = 200). Juice (300 > 200) survives. The
benchmark is not recomputed from only the qualifying row.
Why is Juice the final row?
The saved query orders by CategoryID ascending, then Sale_Price descending. Only Juice qualifies in this
sample, so the final result contains one row. The category average includes all known Beverages prices, not
just rows that survive the comparison.
Final: 1 qualifying product · 3 prices in the benchmark · 1 output row
Source key: blue = Products · No join keys or additional tables are needed for this single-source task.
